statement: Purchased CDS protection exhibits wrong-way risk merely because it gains value when the reference entity's spread widens, regardless of the protection seller's credit quality.
explanation: Wrong-way risk needs a positive link between the exposure and the counterparty's default probability. A rising CDS value alone is not enough; otherwise every hedge would count as wrong-way risk.
originalText: Both CDS trades show WWR, because any purchased protection gains value when the reference spread widens.

statement: A purchased CDS shows wrong-way risk when the protection seller's default probability rises in the same scenario that raises the CDS's value, for example when the seller's loan book is concentrated in the same sector as the reference entity.
explanation: Wrong-way risk exists when exposure and counterparty default probability rise together. A seller whose credit quality depends on the same stress that hurts the reference entity has this link, whereas a diversified seller does not.
originalText: The CDS with Seller Y shows WWR, whereas the CDS with Seller X does not.

statement: Out-of-the-money long put options carry more wrong-way risk than in-the-money long put options.
explanation: An out-of-the-money put has little exposure today and gains value mainly in a severe market fall, which is when the writer is most likely to default. Exposure and default probability are therefore more strongly linked than for an in-the-money put.
originalText: Out‑of‑the‑money put options have more WWR than in‑the‑money put options.

statement: Out-of-the-money put options have less wrong-way risk than in-the-money put options.
explanation: The relationship is the other way round. An out-of-the-money put pays off mainly in a stress scenario, so its exposure is more tightly tied to the writer's default than an in-the-money put, which already has exposure.
originalText: Out‑of‑the‑money put options have less WWR than in‑the‑money put options.
correction: Out-of-the-money put options have more wrong-way risk than in-the-money put options.

statement: A long put option is subject to wrong-way risk if both the risk exposure and the counterparty default probability decrease.
explanation: Wrong-way risk arises when exposure rises as the counterparty's default probability rises. Both falling together is not the definition.
originalText: A long put option is subject to WWR if both risk exposure and counterparty default probability decrease.
correction: A long put option is subject to wrong-way risk if both the risk exposure and the counterparty default probability increase.

statement: When exposure can increase suddenly, collateral might not provide significant mitigation against wrong-way risk.
explanation: Collateral only helps if it can be called and received before default. A sudden jump in exposure leaves no time to collect more, especially when the collateral is itself wrong-way, so the benefit is very limited.
originalText: The potential for a sudden increase in exposure means collateral might not provide significant mitigation against WWR.

statement: A rapid increase in exposure enhances the role of collateral in mitigating wrong-way risk.
explanation: A rapid increase in exposure reduces the role of collateral, because extra collateral cannot be called and received in time. Collateral works best when exposure builds gradually.
originalText: A rapid increase in exposure will enhance the role of collateral in mitigating WWR.
correction: A rapid increase in exposure reduces the role of collateral in mitigating wrong-way risk.

statement: Collateral effectively counterbalances any wrong-way risk, regardless of the speed of the exposure increase.
explanation: Collateral is not a universal offset. Its effectiveness depends strongly on timing, and a rapid exposure jump, or collateral that loses value in the same stress, can leave most of the exposure uncovered.
originalText: Collateral will effectively counterbalance any WWR, regardless of the speed of exposure increase.

statement: The effectiveness of margin against wrong-way risk is timing-dependent: only if exposure increases gradually before default can margin be received and offer a mitigation benefit.
explanation: Margin reduces exposure only to the extent it is actually received before default. If exposure builds gradually, margin can be called and received. If exposure jumps near default, the benefit is very limited.
originalText: Margin’s effectiveness is timing‑dependent, and only if the exposure increases gradually prior to default can margin be received and offer a risk mitigation benefit for WWR.

statement: Margin can effectively mitigate wrong-way risk regardless of market conditions, because it is a buffer that absorbs exposure increases irrespective of timing.
explanation: Timing matters. Margin cannot be received instantly, so a sudden jump in exposure between margin calls or just before default is not covered.
originalText: Margin can effectively mitigate WWR regardless of market conditions, as it serves as a buffer that absorbs potential increases in exposure, irrespective of the timing.

statement: When collateral is negatively correlated with the exposure it secures (wrong-way collateral), the dollar volatility of the net position can exceed that of the unhedged exposure.
explanation: Net position volatility depends on the variances of exposure and collateral and on their correlation. With a negative correlation the collateral loses value as the exposure rises, so it adds variance instead of hedging it.
originalText: Scenario C; \$80.0 million collateral with ρ = ‑0.290

statement: Bonds issued by a wholly owned subsidiary of a CDS reference entity are wrong-way collateral, because they are likely to fall sharply in value just as the reference entity's default makes the CDS exposure jump.
explanation: Collateral issued by an entity closely tied to the reference entity loses value exactly when the exposure it secures rises. Because the exposure jumps rather than builds gradually, extra collateral cannot be called in time and little protection remains.
originalText: The DEF Inc. bonds will fall sharply just as the CDS exposure jumps, so the collateral will cover only a small part of the exposure.

statement: When a parent company defaults, bonds issued by its wholly owned subsidiary are likely to rise in value as investors move into related debt.
explanation: A parent's default signals distress across the group, so a subsidiary's bonds are likely to fall, not rise. This dependence is what makes such bonds wrong-way collateral.
originalText: The DEF Inc. bonds will rise in value as investors move into related debt, so the collateral will exceed the CDS exposure.

statement: A dealer that pays fixed on an interest rate swap and holds government bonds as collateral has wrong-way collateral, because a rise in interest rates increases the swap's value to the dealer while reducing the value of the bonds.
explanation: A pay-fixed swap gains value when rates rise, so the dealer's exposure increases. Government bond prices fall when rates rise, so the collateral loses value at the same time, which is wrong-way collateral.
originalText: It is wrong‑way collateral, because a rise in interest rates increases the swap’s value to the dealer while reducing the value of the government bonds held.

statement: A dealer that receives fixed on an interest rate swap and holds government bonds as collateral has wrong-way collateral, because a fall in rates raises the exposure and reduces the bonds' value.
explanation: For a receive-fixed swap a fall in rates raises the swap's value, but it also raises government bond prices. Exposure and collateral value rise together, which is a favourable (right-way) arrangement.
originalText: It would be wrong‑way collateral if the dealer were instead receiving fixed, because a fall in rates would then raise the exposure and reduce the bonds’ value.

statement: Government bonds posted as collateral against a pay-fixed interest rate swap are right-way collateral, because their high credit quality means they retain their value in a rate shock.
explanation: Credit quality is not the issue. Bond values and swap exposure both depend on interest rates, and for a pay-fixed swap they move in opposite directions: a rate rise raises the exposure and lowers the collateral value.
originalText: It is right‑way collateral, because government bonds are high quality and so retain their value in a rate shock.

statement: When a counterparty posts its own bonds as collateral, the bonds are likely to fall in value as its credit quality deteriorates, so the collateral weakens exactly as its default probability rises.
explanation: Own-issuer bonds are a specific example of wrong-way collateral, because the collateral value is tied directly to the poster's own credit quality.
originalText: The value of the bonds is likely to fall when the counterparty’s credit quality deteriorates, so the collateral weakens exactly as the default probability rises.

statement: There is no wrong-way risk when a counterparty posts its own bonds as collateral, provided the bonds are liquid and valued daily at market prices.
explanation: Liquidity and daily valuation do not remove the link. The bonds still lose value as the issuer's credit deteriorates, which is when protection is needed most.
originalText: There is none, because the counterparty’s own bonds are liquid and are valued daily at market prices.

statement: Higher initial margin at a central counterparty reduces exposure and CVA to a defaulting member but does not eliminate wrong-way risk, because extreme market moves and difficulty auctioning a defaulted portfolio can still produce losses exceeding the margin.
explanation: Initial margin covers potential exposure only up to a finite confidence level. Large, correlated market moves at default, or an illiquid auction of the defaulter's portfolio, can exhaust it and pass losses on to default funds.
originalText: It reduces exposure and the CVA to the defaulter, but does not eliminate WWR, because extreme market moves and difficulty auctioning a defaulted portfolio can still produce losses exceeding the margin.

statement: Initial margin eliminates a central counterparty's wrong-way risk entirely, because continuous full collateralization removes any possibility of loss to the CCP or its clearing members.
explanation: Margin reduces exposure towards zero but not to zero, since it is set at a high but finite coverage level. Losses beyond margin, as in the Nasdaq default, can reach default fund contributions of non-defaulting members.
originalText: It eliminates WWR entirely, because continuous full collateralization removes any possibility of loss to the CCP or its clearing members.

statement: A central counterparty should impose higher haircuts on collateral such as bonds issued by the posting member or its affiliates, because their value is likely to fall exactly when the posting member is more likely to default.
explanation: Own-issuer bonds are wrong-way collateral. Higher haircuts discount them more heavily so the loss waterfall remains adequate if the member defaults.
originalText: Impose higher haircuts on such assets, since their value is likely to fall exactly when the posting member is more likely to default.

statement: A central counterparty should apply lower haircuts to bonds issued by the posting member or its affiliates, since a larger accepted collateral value reduces its exposure to the member.
explanation: Lower haircuts credit the bonds with more value than they will have at default, which worsens the shortfall. Wrong-way collateral calls for higher haircuts.
originalText: Apply lower haircuts to the bonds, since a larger accepted collateral value reduces the exposure to the member.

statement: Wrong-way risk tends to increase with credit quality, so a central counterparty that sets margin mainly from portfolio market risk implicitly ignores it and should arguably require higher margin and default fund contributions from stronger, more systemic members.
explanation: A large, strong dealer implies more wrong-way risk, but margin based on market risk disassociates credit quality from exposure. Stronger and more systemic members therefore arguably warrant higher margin and default fund contributions.
originalText: She is incorrect, because WWR tends to increase with credit quality, so the CCP implicitly ignores it and should arguably require higher margin and default fund contributions from stronger, more systemic members.

statement: Wrong-way risk falls as a clearing member's credit quality rises, so central counterparties should require less margin from stronger members.
explanation: The relationship is the opposite: wrong-way risk tends to increase with credit quality, because a default of a strong, systemic member is associated with a large jump in exposure.
originalText: She is incorrect, because WWR falls as the credit quality of a member rises, so CCPs should require less margin from stronger members.

statement: Wrong-way risk is incorporated into the standard CVA formula by replacing the unconditional expected exposure with the expected exposure conditional on default of the counterparty.
explanation: The standard formula multiplies unconditional expected exposure by default probability, which assumes independence. Using exposure conditional on default captures the dependence while keeping the formula's structure.
originalText: Replace EE(t) with the expected exposure conditional on default of the counterparty.

statement: The standard CVA expression cannot be adjusted for wrong-way risk and cannot be used when wrong-way risk is present.
explanation: The formula remains usable. It only requires exposure conditional on counterparty default, for example from a hazard rate approach, in place of unconditional expected exposure.
originalText: No adjustment is possible; the expression cannot be used when wrong‑way risk is present.

statement: Jump approaches account for abrupt changes in exposure, which is critical for capturing the risk of sudden market shifts.
explanation: Jump approaches assume the exposure driver, such as an FX rate, jumps at the counterparty's default, so they capture sudden exposure increases that continuous approaches understate.
originalText: Jump approaches, since they account for abrupt changes in exposure, which is critical for capturing the risk of sudden market shifts.

statement: Hazard rate approaches are ideal for precise estimation of wrong-way risk, because they offer transparent and easily calibrated correlation parameters.
explanation: Hazard rate (intensity) approaches are easy to implement but generally imply only weak dependence between default and exposure, so they tend to underestimate wrong-way risk.
originalText: Hazard rate approaches, as they offer transparent correlation parameters that are easy to calibrate, making them ideal for precise WWR estimation.

statement: Jump approaches tend to show collateralization as nearly useless when exposure jumps at default.
explanation: The jump approach models exposure gapping at default, leaving no time for margin to be collected. This matches the observed ineffectiveness of collateral under stress.
originalText: Jump approaches, because they tend to show collateralization as nearly useless when exposure jumps at default.

statement: Wrong-way risk is not materially affected by how quickly exposure increases relative to margin calls.
explanation: Collateral effectiveness is very timing dependent. If exposure rises faster than margin can be called and received, collateral gives little protection.
originalText: Hudson’s current approach is adequate, because WWR is not materially affected by how quickly exposure increases relative to margin calls.

statement: The jump approach to wrong-way risk assumes the relevant FX rate jumps by a factor related to a residual value at the counterparty's default time, and the jump is typically larger for highly rated, systemically important sovereigns.
explanation: The jump approach is defined by a discrete move in the exposure driver at default. Evidence shows larger jumps for large firms and highly rated sovereigns because their default is a more significant shock.
originalText: It assumes the relevant FX rate jumps by a factor related to a residual value at the counterparty’s default time; the jump is typically larger for highly rated, systemically important sovereigns.

statement: The hazard rate approach simulates a stochastic process for credit spreads and computes conditional exposure on paths where default occurs; it is the easiest method but tends to overstate wrong-way risk.
explanation: The hazard rate (intensity) approach is easy to implement but generally shows weak dependence between default and exposure, so it tends to understate wrong-way risk.
originalText: It simulates a stochastic process for credit spreads and computes conditional exposure on paths where default occurs; it is the easiest method but tends to overstate WWR.
correction: The hazard rate approach simulates a stochastic process for credit spreads and computes conditional exposure on paths where default occurs; it is the easiest method but tends to understate wrong-way risk.

statement: A waterfall in a securitization is the set of rules on how cash flows from the collateral are distributed to the various securities in the capital structure.
explanation: The waterfall allocates collateral cash flows, after fees and costs, to the tranches in order of seniority from the top down, with the residual going to equity.
originalText: Rules on how cash flows from the collateral are distributed to the various securities in the capital structure

statement: A waterfall in a securitization is the process of creating a securitized credit product.
explanation: That describes securitization itself: pooling credit-sensitive assets and issuing new securities backed by them. The waterfall is only one feature of the structure, namely its payment priority rules.
originalText: The process of creating a securitized credit product

statement: A waterfall in a securitization is a financial intermediary that aggregates the underlying loans and designs the securitization structure.
explanation: An intermediary that pools the loans and designs the deal is the arranger or underwriter (or the special purpose vehicle). The waterfall is the set of payment priority rules.
originalText: A financial intermediary that aggregates underlying loans and designs the securitization structure

statement: When interest collected on a securitization's collateral falls short of the coupons due, the senior and mezzanine tranches share the shortfall pro rata to their coupons.
explanation: A waterfall is sequential, not pro rata. The senior coupon is paid in full first, so the shortfall falls on the mezzanine tranche and nothing is left for equity or the trust account.
originalText: The senior and mezzanine tranches share the \$0.6 million shortfall pro rata to their coupons, so each is paid slightly less than its promised coupon.

statement: When interest collected on a securitization's collateral is insufficient to pay the senior and mezzanine coupons in full, the equity holders fund the shortfall.
explanation: Equity holders are residual claimants with no obligation to fund shortfalls. When cash is insufficient they simply receive nothing, and the shortfall falls on the most junior bond tranche paid.
originalText: The senior and mezzanine tranches are paid in full, with the \$0.6 million shortfall funded by the equity holders.

statement: In the standard Malz three-tier securitization example, recovered funds from defaulted loans are paid out to the equity holders each year as they are received.
explanation: In the interim years recoveries are deposited into the overcollateralization account together with the diverted excess spread, where they earn interest. Equity receives only the excess spread left after the diversion.
originalText: Recovered funds are paid out to the equity holders each year as they are received.
correction: In the standard Malz three-tier securitization example, recovered funds from defaulted loans are deposited into the overcollateralization account each year as they are received.

changes.from: paid out to the equity holders

statement: In a securitization where excess spread is diverted to an overcollateralization account up to a maximum annual amount K, any excess spread above K is paid to the equity noteholders.
explanation: The cap limits how much soft credit enhancement is built each year. The remainder, the excess spread less K, is released as residual cash flow to equity.
originalText: It is paid to the equity noteholders.

statement: In a securitization where excess spread is diverted to an overcollateralization account up to a maximum annual amount K, any excess spread above K is also deposited in the overcollateralization account.
explanation: If all excess spread were retained there would be no cap. Only K goes to the overcollateralization account each year, and the amount above K goes to equity.
originalText: It is also deposited in the OC account to further enhance credit quality.

statement: In a securitization with an overcollateralization account, excess spread above the annual cap is used to repay the principal of the senior bonds.
explanation: Excess spread is not used to amortize senior principal in the interim years. Principal is repaid at maturity, and surplus above the cap is the equity tranche's residual.
originalText: It is used to repay the principal of the senior bonds.

statement: In a securitization with overcollateralization, up to a maximum annual amount K of positive excess spread is diverted to the overcollateralization account to absorb future shortfalls, and any remainder goes to equity.
explanation: Excess spread is soft credit enhancement. It is first used to build a reserve, up to K per year, that can pay bond coupons in later years when excess spread turns negative, with equity receiving the residual.
originalText: Up to a maximum annual amount $K$ is diverted to the OC account to absorb future shortfalls, and any remainder goes to equity.

statement: In a securitization with overcollateralization, all positive excess spread is paid to the equity tranche each year.
explanation: Excess spread first goes to the overcollateralization account, up to the annual cap K, to protect the bonds. Only the remainder above the cap is paid to equity.
originalText: All excess spread is paid to the equity tranche each year.

statement: In a three-tier securitization, positive excess spread is shared equally among the senior, mezzanine and equity tranches.
explanation: Bond tranches receive only their contractual coupons. Excess spread is not distributed equally; it builds the overcollateralization account and then goes to equity.
originalText: Excess spread is shared equally among senior, mezzanine and equity tranches.

statement: The default ratio of a credit card ABS is the value of credit card receivables written off during the period as a proportion of total credit card receivables.
explanation: The default ratio measures realised credit losses (charge-offs) relative to the receivables pool. Together with the delinquency ratio it indicates the pool's credit loss.
originalText: The value of credit card receivables written off during the period as a proportion of total credit card receivables.

statement: The default ratio of a credit card ABS is the value of credit card receivables overdue by more than 90 days as a proportion of total credit card receivables.
explanation: That is the delinquency ratio, an early-warning measure. The default ratio is based on receivables actually written off.
originalText: The value of credit card receivables overdue by more than 90 days as a proportion of total credit card receivables.
correction: The delinquency ratio of a credit card ABS is the value of credit card receivables overdue by more than 90 days as a proportion of total credit card receivables.

statement: The default ratio of a credit card ABS is the proportion of the pool's interest and principal that is repaid in a particular period.
explanation: That is the monthly payment rate (MPR), a measure of payment speed. The default ratio measures written-off receivables as a proportion of the receivables pool.
originalText: The proportion of the pool’s interest and principal that is repaid in a particular period.
correction: The monthly payment rate of a credit card ABS is the proportion of the pool's interest and principal that is repaid in a particular period.

statement: The default ratio of a credit card ABS is the value of credit card receivables written off as a proportion of total liabilities.
explanation: The denominator is the receivables pool, not total liabilities. The default ratio is written-off receivables divided by total credit card receivables.
originalText: The value of credit card receivables written off as a proportion of total liabilities.
correction: The default ratio of a credit card ABS is the value of credit card receivables written off as a proportion of total credit card receivables.

statement: The single monthly mortality rate (SMM) under 100% PSA is exactly 50% of the SMM under 200% PSA.
explanation: PSA scales the CPR, and SMM is a compounded transformation of CPR, so doubling the PSA multiple does not exactly double SMM. After month 30, SMM is about 0.514% at 100% PSA and about 1.060% at 200% PSA, a ratio of roughly 48.5%.
originalText: The single monthly mortality rate (SMM) under 100% PSA is exactly 50% of the SMM under 200% PSA

statement: The PSA benchmark assumes lower prepayment rates for young mortgage pools.
explanation: The PSA ramp starts at a low CPR and rises with the age of the pool, so young pools prepay slowly.
originalText: PSA assumes lower prepayment rates for young mortgage pools

statement: 100% PSA assumes a CPR of 0.2% for the first month, increasing by 0.2% per month for the next 29 months when it reaches 6% per year, and remaining at 6% per year thereafter.
explanation: This is the standard definition of the 100% PSA ramp: 0.2% times 30 months gives the 6% plateau.
originalText: 100% PSA assumes a CPR of 0.2% for the first month, increasing by 0.2% per month for the next 29 months when it reaches 6% per year, and remains at 6% per year thereafter

statement: At month 30, the remaining principal of a mortgage pool is lower under a 150% PSA assumption than under 100% PSA.
explanation: A faster speed means a higher CPR in every month, so more principal has been prepaid by month 30 and the remaining balance is lower.
originalText: At month 30, the remaining principal of a mortgage pool will be lower under a 150% PSA assumption than under 100% PSA

statement: A 200% PSA prepayment speed implies a CPR of 12% at month 30, which corresponds to an SMM of about 1.06%, since $\text{SMM} = 1 - (1 - \text{CPR})^{1/12}$.
explanation: At month 30, 100% PSA gives a CPR of 6%, so 200% PSA gives 12%. Converting with the compounding formula gives $1 - 0.88^{1/12} \approx 1.06\%$, not 12% divided by 12.
originalText: At month 30 under 200% PSA, the SMM is about 1.06%, equal to $1 - (1 - 2 \times6\%)^{1/12}$.

statement: Raising the prepayment speed assumption on a pass-through MBS from 200% PSA to 250% PSA would lengthen the security's weighted average life.
explanation: A higher PSA means faster prepayments, which return principal sooner and shorten the weighted average life.
originalText: Raising the assumption to 250% PSA would lengthen the security’s weighted average life (WAL).
correction: Raising the prepayment speed assumption on a pass-through MBS from 200% PSA to 250% PSA would shorten the security's weighted average life.

statement: At month 30 under 200% PSA, the CPR is 6%.
explanation: 6% is the month-30 CPR under 100% PSA. Under 200% PSA the CPR is twice that, 12%.
correction: At month 30 under 200% PSA, the CPR is 12%.

statement: The risk that residential mortgages and other consumer loans pooled as collateral are terminated or paid off ahead of schedule is known as prepayment risk.
explanation: Early repayment of pooled loans changes the timing of the expected cash flows and the weighted average life of the securitization.
originalText: Prepayment risk

statement: The 100% PSA benchmark has a CPR that rises by 0.2% each month until it reaches 6% in month 30, and stays at 6% thereafter.
explanation: The 100% PSA benchmark ramps CPR by 0.2% per month over 30 months to a 6% plateau. Other PSA speeds scale this path proportionally.
originalText: A 100% PSA pool has a CPR that starts at 0% and rises by 0.2% each month until it reaches 6% in month 30, and stays at 6% thereafter.

statement: The 100% PSA benchmark has a CPR that rises by 0.2% each month until it reaches 6% in month 60, and stays at 6% thereafter.
explanation: The ramp lasts 30 months, since 0.2% times 30 equals 6%. Reaching 6% in 60 months would require only 0.1% per month.
originalText: A 100% PSA pool has a CPR that starts at 0% and rises by 0.2% each month until it reaches 6% in month 60, and stays at 6% thereafter.
correction: The 100% PSA benchmark has a CPR that rises by 0.2% each month until it reaches 6% in month 30, and stays at 6% thereafter.

statement: A monthly SMM of 0.65% implies an annual CPR of exactly 12 times 0.65%, or 7.80%.
explanation: CPR compounds SMM rather than multiplying it by 12. The CPR is $1-(1-0.0065)^{12} \approx 7.53\%$.
originalText: A monthly SMM of 0.65% implies an annual CPR of exactly 12 × 0.65% = 7.80%.

statement: A 150% PSA pool has a CPR that rises by 0.2% each month and reaches a plateau of 9% in month 45.
explanation: 150% PSA scales the 100% PSA path by 1.5, so CPR rises by 0.3% per month and reaches a 9% plateau in month 30.
correction: A 150% PSA pool has a CPR that rises by 0.3% each month and reaches a plateau of 9% in month 30.

statement: According to GARP, the chief executive officer is the real head of risk management, must make the whole organization respect risk management principles, and must involve the risk management function in strategic decisions.
explanation: Appointing an independent CRO adds a second line of defense but does not move the CEO's responsibility. In strategic decisions such as mergers and acquisitions the CEO involves risk management at the right time.
originalText: Not quite: the CEO is the real head of risk management, must make the whole bank respect its principles and must involve risk in strategy.

statement: Once an independent CRO heading the second line is appointed, the CRO becomes accountable for the bank's risk profile and the CEO's part is limited to approving the guidelines.
explanation: The CEO's responsibility for risk management is neither limited nor transferred to the CRO. The board, not the CEO, approves the risk guidelines.
originalText: Agreed: the CRO is now accountable for the bank’s risk profile, and the CEO’s part is limited to approving the guidelines.

statement: The CEO should stay out of risk decisions so that the independence of the second line from management is kept.
explanation: The second line is independent of the business, not of management. The CEO must involve risk management in decisions, not avoid it.
originalText: Agreed: the CEO should stay out of risk decisions, so that the independence of the second line from management is kept.

statement: For IT security as a hybrid function, encrypting data and partitioning the network are first-line roles, while verifying ICT controls and enforcing security policies are second-line roles.
explanation: Regulators require hybrid functions to document and distinguish their first-line and second-line responsibilities, emphasising the independence of the second line.
originalText: In IT security, encrypting data and partitioning the network are documented as first-line roles, while verifying ICT controls and enforcing security policies are documented as second-line roles.

statement: In the three lines of defence model, the second line gives the final sign-off on a business unit's risk and control self-assessment, because the second line owns the methodology.
explanation: The first line owns the risks it generates and gives the final sign-off on its assessment. The second line owns the methodology and the challenge, and stays independent of the content.
originalText: A second-line risk manager facilitates each business unit’s risk and control self-assessment and gives the final sign-off on its results, as the second line owns the methodology.

statement: Risk champions can take over ownership of their department's operational risks, so that the head of the department can concentrate on running the business.
explanation: Risk champions (the so-called line 1.5) record events, map risks and controls and follow up action plans inside the business. Ownership of operational risk must stay with business managers and must not pass to them.
originalText: The payments department’s risk champions take over ownership of the department’s operational risks, so that the head of payments can concentrate on running the business.

statement: Once internal audit has evaluated the corporate operational risk function as effective, it can rely exclusively on that function's control testing when auditing a business department.
explanation: A positive evaluation can justify less intense scrutiny, but internal audit never relies exclusively on the work of risk, compliance or finance. It always examines its own sample.
originalText: After evaluating the corporate operational risk function as effective, internal audit relies exclusively on that function’s control testing when auditing the payments department.

statement: Economic capital at the loan level equals the loan's unexpected loss contribution times the capital multiplier, which reflects diversification, unlike a regulatory approach that assigns roughly 8% capital to each credit on a standalone basis.
explanation: Loan-level economic capital is proportional to the loan's contribution to portfolio credit risk. The regulatory approach instead assigns roughly 8% equity capital to each credit standalone.
originalText: Economic capital at the loan level equals the loan’s unexpected loss contribution times the capital multiplier, which reflects diversification, unlike a regulatory approach assigning roughly 8% capital to each credit standalone.

statement: A bank targeting a higher credit rating can choose a lower confidence level, which lowers the capital multiplier applied to unexpected loss and so reduces the economic capital it must hold.
explanation: A bank targeting a very high rating must choose a very high confidence level, such as 99.97%, which corresponds to a higher capital multiplier and so more economic capital.
correction: A bank targeting a higher credit rating must choose a higher confidence level, which raises the capital multiplier applied to unexpected loss and so increases the economic capital it must hold.

statement: Economic capital is calculated with industrywide rules and formulas and sets only a minimum level of capital adequacy, whereas regulatory capital reflects the bank's own estimate of its risk.
explanation: The labels are swapped. Regulatory capital follows industrywide rules and sets a minimum, while economic capital is the bank's own estimate intended to capture the economic realities of the risks it runs.
originalText: Economic capital is calculated with industrywide rules and formulas and sets only a minimum level of capital adequacy, whereas regulatory capital reflects the bank’s own estimate of its risk.
correction: Regulatory capital is calculated with industrywide rules and formulas and sets only a minimum level of capital adequacy, whereas economic capital reflects the bank's own estimate of its risk.

statement: Economic capital for credit risk is the capital needed to absorb the expected loss plus the unexpected loss up to the confidence level, so it is measured from zero loss rather than from expected loss.
explanation: Expected loss is the foreseeable cost of doing business, covered by pricing and loan loss reserves. Economic capital is the distance between the expected loss and the unexpected loss at the chosen confidence level, so it is measured from expected loss.
originalText: Economic capital for credit risk is the capital needed to absorb the expected loss plus the unexpected loss up to the confidence level, so it is measured from zero loss rather than from EL.

statement: Altman's Z-score is a linear discriminant function: five accounting ratios are combined with fixed weights estimated from samples of failed and non-failed firms, and cut-off values of Z assign each firm to a group.
explanation: The weights come from the data (Altman 1968 used 33 failed and 33 non-failed manufacturers), so the Z-score is an empirical model. Cut-offs of Z place the firm in a credit-quality group.
originalText: The Z-score is a linear discriminant function: five accounting ratios are combined with fixed weights estimated from samples of failed and non-failed firms, and cut-off values of $Z$ assign each firm to a group.

statement: The Altman Z-score is a structural financial model whose weights come from option pricing theory, and Z measures how many standard deviations the firm's assets are above the default point.
explanation: That describes Merton's distance to default. The Z-score has no option-pricing content and no default point; it is a discriminant function of accounting ratios.
originalText: The Z-score is a structural financial model: its weights come from option pricing theory, and $Z$ measures how many standard deviations the firm’s assets are above the default point.

statement: In a credit-scoring context, LDA refers to the loss distribution approach, which combines a frequency and a severity distribution of losses into the firm's score.
explanation: The loss distribution approach is an operational-risk capital method. In credit scoring, LDA stands for linear discriminant analysis.
originalText: In a credit-scoring context, “LDA” refers to the loss distribution approach, which combines a frequency and a severity distribution of losses into the firm’s score.

statement: A higher Altman Z-score signals a higher likelihood of default, because each of the five accounting ratios enters the score with a negative weight.
explanation: Every weight is positive, so a higher Z signals lower default risk.
originalText: A higher Z-score signals a higher likelihood of default, because each of the five accounting ratios enters the score with a negative weight.
correction: A higher Altman Z-score signals a lower likelihood of default, because each of the five accounting ratios enters the score with a positive weight.

statement: Merton's distance-to-default model cannot be applied to debt with a maturity beyond one year.
explanation: Distance to default is defined for default T years in the future, and the drift scales with T while volatility scales with the square root of T. Nothing limits the model to one year.
originalText: The short-form distance to default is about 2.03, placing the borrower in band BB; the same scoring step could not be used for its three-year notes, because Merton’s model cannot be applied beyond one year.

statement: A rise in asset volatility increases a borrower's distance to default, which supports an upgrade in its internal rating band.
explanation: Higher asset volatility lowers the distance to default, since DD is roughly the log of assets over default point divided by volatility. A lower DD means the firm is more likely to default.
originalText: The short-form distance to default is about 2.03, placing the borrower in band BB; a rise in asset volatility to 25% would increase the distance to default and support an upgrade toward BBB.
correction: A rise in asset volatility reduces a borrower's distance to default, which supports a downgrade in its internal rating band.

statement: Moody's KMV converts a distance to default into a default probability by reading $N(-\text{DD})$ off the standard normal distribution.
explanation: Mapping through the normal distribution is the plain Merton approach. Moody's KMV uses historical data to derive an empirical distribution of default frequencies for each distance to default.
originalText: The short-form distance to default is about 2.03, placing the borrower in band BB; Moody’s KMV would convert the same score into a default probability by reading $N(-\text{DD})$ off the standard normal distribution.

statement: A hazard rate implied by credit spreads is a risk-neutral estimate that includes compensation for bearing default risk, mainly systematic risk, so it should be used to value bonds but not to forecast how many issuers will actually default.
explanation: Spread-implied hazard rates exceed historical default-based (real-world) rates because investors are paid for systematic risk, illiquidity and hard-to-diversify risk. Use risk-neutral rates for valuation and real-world rates for forecasting actual defaults.
originalText: The 4.7% is a risk-neutral estimate that includes compensation for bearing default risk, mainly systematic risk, so it should be used to value the bonds but not to forecast how many BB issuers will actually default.

statement: Hazard rates implied by market credit spreads are real-world estimates, whereas hazard rates implied by historical default experience are risk-neutral estimates.
explanation: The labels are reversed. Market-implied estimates are risk-neutral, and estimates based on historical default frequencies are real-world.
originalText: The 4.7% is a real-world estimate because it comes from current market prices, while the 1.3% is a stale risk-neutral estimate that should be discarded.
correction: Hazard rates implied by market credit spreads are risk-neutral estimates, whereas hazard rates implied by historical default experience are real-world estimates.

statement: When the spread-implied hazard rate exceeds the historical default-implied hazard rate, an investor can buy the bonds, buy CDS protection and lock in a riskless profit equal to the difference in hazard rates.
explanation: Buying the bond and protection hedges default risk away and earns roughly the risk-free rate. The gap between the two hazard rates is a premium for bearing risk, not a riskless profit.
originalText: The gap is an arbitrage: an investor can buy the bonds, buy CDS protection, and lock in a riskless profit equal to the difference in hazard rates.

statement: The gap between spread-implied and historical-default-implied hazard rates is smaller for B and CCC/C issuers than for BB issuers, because riskier bonds are priced closer to their actuarial cost of default.
explanation: The gap widens as credit quality falls, because excess returns rise with credit risk. In GARP's table it is about 4.65 percentage points for B and 8.28 for CCC/C.
originalText: The gap should be smaller for B and CCC/C issuers, because riskier bonds are priced closer to their actuarial cost of default.

statement: In the Basel IRB implementation of Vasicek's model, downgrade risk enters through the maturity adjustment, because Vasicek's model itself counts only defaults.
explanation: Vasicek's model estimates the loss distribution arising from defaults and ignores downgrades. In the regulatory implementation, the maturity adjustment allows for the effect of downgrades.
originalText: In the IRB implementation, the maturity adjustment is the channel through which downgrade risk enters, because Vasicek’s model itself counts defaults only.

statement: Vasicek's model captures losses from both downgrades and defaults, which is why regulators chose it for IRB capital.
explanation: A model that captures downgrades as well as defaults is CreditMetrics. Vasicek's model counts defaults only.
originalText: Vasicek’s model captures losses from both downgrades and defaults, which is why regulators chose it for IRB capital.

statement: Because it uses a Gaussian copula, Vasicek's model generates strong tail dependence between defaults in a crisis.
explanation: The Gaussian copula incorporates very little tail correlation. A different copula is needed to add tail dependence.
originalText: Because it uses a Gaussian copula, Vasicek’s model generates strong tail dependence between defaults in a crisis.
correction: Because it uses a Gaussian copula, Vasicek's model generates very little tail dependence between defaults in a crisis.

statement: Under Advanced IRB, each bank sets the correlation in Vasicek's model from the equity-return correlations of its own obligors.
explanation: Under both Foundation and Advanced IRB the correlation is set by the Basel formula for each asset class. Equity correlations are used to calibrate a bank's own economic capital model.
originalText: Under Advanced IRB each bank sets the correlation $\rho$ from the equity-return correlations of its own obligors.

statement: Daily portfolio reconciliation reduces margin disputes, and a history of disputes is one reason Basel III requires a longer margin period of risk, which raises capital and rewards lower operational risk.
explanation: Reconciliation aims to minimise disputes by agreeing valuations and margin requirements. Basel III requires a larger MPoR for netting sets with a history of margin call disputes, which gives an incentive to reduce operational risk.
originalText: Daily portfolio reconciliation reduces margin disputes, and a history of disputes is one reason Basel III requires a longer MPoR, raising capital and rewarding lower operational risk.

statement: A rating-based break clause offers the same benefits as a mandatory break: counterparty risk reduction, CVA reduction, capital relief and LCR relief.
explanation: Only mandatory breaks give all four benefits. A rating-based break gives at most some counterparty risk reduction, Basel rules out capital relief from rating triggers, and the LCR requires banks to pre-fund them.

statement: Liquidity risk from holding non-cash margin falls on the margin giver, which bears the bid-offer costs and price falls when the securities are sold after a default.
explanation: Liquidation risk sits with the non-defaulting party that holds the margin and must sell it for cash to rehedge, and haircuts are set to cover it. The giver's risk is funding liquidity risk when it must post.
correction: Liquidity risk from holding non-cash margin falls on the margin holder, which bears the bid-offer costs and price falls when the securities are sold after a default.

statement: Because a compression cycle lowers the total notional of all participants, it guarantees that each participant ends with a lower notional to every counterparty.
explanation: Compression reduces the total notional of all parties, but an individual party does not necessarily end with a lower notional to each counterparty. Positions between pairs can even rise or change sign.

statement: Variation margin and initial margin transfers can be netted against each other into a single net amount.
explanation: Initial margin is computed separately as an independent amount, may be segregated, and is not netted with variation margin. The two are transferred separately, possibly in opposite directions.
originalText: The hedge fund delivers a single net amount of USD 27 million.

statement: Initial margin is a static amount fixed at inception of a trade rather than recalculated over time.
explanation: The term may suggest a static quantity, but initial margin is now recalculated over time, for example daily, from the risk of the portfolio. If the requirement falls, the excess is returned.
originalText: The hedge fund delivers USD 35 million of variation margin; the initial margin stays at USD 60 million because it is fixed at inception.

statement: When the required initial margin falls below the amount held, the excess initial margin is returned in a transfer separate from any variation margin call.
explanation: Variation margin tracks the value of the portfolio, while initial margin tracks its riskiness. They are computed and transferred separately.
originalText: The hedge fund delivers USD 35 million of variation margin, and the dealer separately returns USD 8 million of initial margin.

statement: A two-way CSA with zero thresholds is the interbank standard and aims to benefit both parties from a counterparty risk point of view.
explanation: Both parties post against a negative value, so both exposures are mitigated.
originalText: Sign a two-way CSA with zero thresholds with the dealer bank, the interbank standard, which aims to benefit both parties on counterparty risk.

statement: A one-way CSA adds risk only for the party that receives the margin.
explanation: A one-way CSA represents additional risk for the margin giver, putting it in a worse position than having no CSA. The receiver is the party that benefits.
originalText: Accept the supranational’s one-way CSA in its favour, since a one-way CSA adds risk only for the party that receives the margin.
correction: A one-way CSA adds risk only for the party that gives the margin.

statement: Linking a counterparty's CSA threshold to its net asset value so that the threshold rises as the net asset value falls is consistent with credit-quality-linked collateral terms.
explanation: Credit-quality links tighten terms (lower thresholds, initial margin) as quality deteriorates. A threshold that rises as net asset value falls would loosen collateralization exactly when risk is highest.
originalText: Link the hedge fund’s threshold to its net asset value so that the threshold rises as the net asset value falls, easing its workload under stress.

statement: Letting both parties act as valuation agent on every CSA removes the potential for disputes over margin calls.
explanation: Where both parties are valuation agents, each calling for margin when it has an exposure, the potential for margin disputes is significant. Reconciliation reduces disputes but nothing removes them.
originalText: Let both parties act as valuation agent on every CSA, since two valuation agents remove the potential for disputes over margin calls.

statement: The liquidity coverage ratio requires a bank to pre-fund the contingent outflow from rating-linked initial margin, for example 2% of notional if it is downgraded to BBB+.
explanation: Basel capital rules give no capital benefit for rating triggers, but the liquidity coverage ratio requires banks to pre-fund ratings-contingent outflows.
originalText: The liquidity coverage ratio requires the bank to pre-fund the contingent outflow, for example 2% initial margin for a three-notch downgrade to BBB+.

statement: Basel capital rules give a bank's counterparties capital relief for rating triggers in collateral agreements, since a downgrade would bring in margin before any default.
explanation: Basel explicitly rules out capital relief from rating triggers and assumes a counterparty defaults without first being downgraded.
originalText: Basel capital rules give the bank’s counterparties capital relief for the triggers, since a downgrade would bring in margin before any default.

statement: Rating-based triggers are effective because rating agencies typically downgrade well before a firm's financial difficulties become acute.
explanation: Ratings are somewhat unreactive. By the time of the downgrade the difficulties may already be too acute, as the monoline insurers showed.
originalText: The triggers are effective because rating agencies typically downgrade well before a firm’s financial diﬀiculties become acute.

statement: Because each counterparty's rating trigger operates separately, a single-notch downgrade can have only a small and gradual effect on a bank's liquidity.
explanation: Triggers create cliff-edge effects: a single-notch downgrade can trigger many counterparties at once, as happened with AIG.
originalText: Because each counterparty’s trigger operates separately, a single-notch downgrade can have only a small and gradual effect on the bank’s liquidity.

statement: Funding liquidity risk falls mainly on the margin giver, which must source eligible collateral within short timescales whenever its position moves further against it.
explanation: End users face funding liquidity risk when posting margin, and may default while solvent if they cannot meet a call in eligible securities.
originalText: Funding liquidity risk falls mainly on the corporate, which must source eligible collateral within short timescales whenever the swap moves further against it.

statement: Liquidation risk falls on the margin giver, which bears the bid-offer cost and price falls if the securities are sold after a default.
explanation: Liquidation risk sits with the margin holder, which must sell the collateral after a default to rehedge.
originalText: Liquidation risk falls on the corporate as margin giver, which bears the bid-offer cost and price falls if the bonds are sold after a default.
correction: Liquidation risk falls on the margin holder, which bears the bid-offer cost and price falls if the securities are sold after a default.

statement: Market risk over the margin period of risk falls on the margin giver, since the margin receiver is fully protected until close-out.
explanation: The margin period of risk is the receiver's uncollateralised period, so the receiver is not protected during it and carries the market risk over it.
originalText: Market risk over the margin period of risk falls on the corporate, since the bank as margin receiver is fully protected until close-out.

statement: Under a two-way CSA with zero thresholds and daily variation margin, exposure remains because margin arrives with a delay over the margin period of risk, and margin posted but not returned when the counterparty defaults is itself a positive exposure.
explanation: Positive exposure is the maximum of portfolio value less margin and zero. Posted margin enters with a negative sign, so margin exceeding what is owed adds exposure, and the delay over the MPoR leaves residual exposure.
originalText: Exposure will remain, because margin arrives with a delay over the margin period of risk, and margin the bank has posted but not had returned when the hedge fund defaults is itself a positive exposure.

statement: Because margin received is subtracted from the portfolio value, a CSA can only reduce a bank's positive exposure, and margin the bank posts can never create exposure to the counterparty.
explanation: Margin posted but not returned is an unsecured claim on a defaulting counterparty. Two-way margin can therefore create exposure as well as reduce it.
originalText: Because margin received is subtracted from the portfolio value, the CSA can only reduce the bank’s positive exposure; margin the bank posts can never create exposure to the hedge fund.

statement: A threshold acts like initial margin, so agreeing a higher threshold moves the collateralization profile from strongly collateralised towards overcollateralised.
explanation: A threshold is a negative initial margin. Raising it moves the profile towards partially collateralised and eventually the uncollateralised case, not towards overcollateralised.
originalText: A threshold acts like initial margin, so agreeing a threshold of EUR 10 million instead of zero would move the profile from strongly collateralised towards overcollateralised.

statement: With zero thresholds and daily calls the exposure profile is close to zero at every horizon, so adding initial margin would bring no further reduction.
explanation: The margin period of risk leaves a material exposure even under strong collateralisation. Initial margin reduces it further and can lead to the overcollateralised case.

statement: With variation margin only, the best-case reduction in exposure from collateralisation is about the square root of maturity over the margin period of risk; in practice it is smaller, and a longer MPoR moves CVA back towards its uncollateralised value.
explanation: Moves scale with the square root of time, so a five-year swap with a 10-day MPoR gives at best about 11 times lower exposure. A longer MPoR, for example 20 days for a large or disputed netting set, reduces that benefit.
originalText: The best-case fall in exposure is about the square root of maturity over MPoR, roughly 11 times; in practice it is smaller, and a longer MPoR (for example 20 days for a large or disputed netting set) moves CVA back towards the uncollateralised value.

statement: With variation margin only, the best-case reduction in exposure from collateralisation is about the ratio of maturity to the margin period of risk.
explanation: That treats exposure as proportional to time. Exposure scales with the square root of time, so the best-case reduction is about the square root of the ratio.
originalText: The best-case fall in exposure is about the ratio of maturity to MPoR, roughly 125 times, because margin covers all but 10 of the 1,250 business days.
correction: With variation margin only, the best-case reduction in exposure from collateralisation is about the square root of the ratio of maturity to the margin period of risk.

changes.to: about the square root of the ratio

statement: Moving to a collateralised CSA reduces CVA because the counterparty's default probability is lower once it posts margin.
explanation: Collateral works on exposure, never on the counterparty's default probability. Margin changes only the expected positive exposure in the CVA formula, while PD and LGD are unchanged.
originalText: CVA falls because the corporate’s default probability is lower once it posts margin; the EPE profile is unchanged.

statement: With a zero threshold and daily margin calls, collateralised CVA is negligible, so it can be set to zero without modelling the margin period of risk.
explanation: The margin period of risk leaves a material residual exposure even with zero thresholds and daily calls, which is why it must be modelled.
originalText: With a zero threshold and daily calls, collateralised CVA is negligible, so the desk can set it to zero without modelling the MPoR.

statement: In a contingent BCVA each own-default (DVA) term is weighted by the counterparty's probability of surviving to the start of the interval, so a widening of the counterparty's credit spread decreases the DVA term while unilateral DVA is unchanged.
explanation: Unilateral DVA depends only on the institution's own LGD, default probability and expected negative exposure. In BCVA the counterparty's survival probability falls as its spread widens, shrinking the DVA term.
originalText: UDVA is unchanged; the DVA term inside BCVA decreases, because each own-default term is weighted by the client’s probability of surviving to the start of the interval.

statement: A wider counterparty credit spread increases the DVA term inside BCVA, because the counterparty's higher default probability makes the institution's liabilities to it worth less.
explanation: The counterparty's credit enters the DVA term only through its survival probability, which falls when its spread widens. The DVA term therefore decreases.
originalText: UDVA is unchanged; the DVA term inside BCVA increases, because the client’s higher default probability makes the bank’s liabilities to it worth less.
correction: A wider counterparty credit spread decreases the DVA term inside BCVA, because the counterparty's higher default probability lowers its probability of surviving to the start of each interval.

changes.from: makes the institution's liabilities to it worth less
changes.to: lowers its probability of surviving to the start of each interval

statement: Survival adjustments in a contingent BCVA apply only to the CVA term and not to the DVA term.
explanation: Survival adjustments apply to both legs: each CVA term is weighted by the institution's own survival and each DVA term by the counterparty's survival.
originalText: UDVA decreases, while the DVA term inside BCVA is unchanged, because survival adjustments apply only to the CVA term.

statement: Including survival probabilities makes the CVA term sensitive to the institution's own credit quality, which may be seen as unnatural and which regulation may prohibit.
explanation: Survival adjustment conditions each default on the other party not having defaulted first, which introduces dependence on the institution's own credit quality.
originalText: Including survival probabilities makes the CVA term sensitive to the institution’s own credit quality, which may be seen as unnatural and which regulation may prohibit.

statement: Including survival probabilities leaves BCVA exactly equal to UCVA plus UDVA, because the reductions in the two legs offset each other.
explanation: Both legs shrink but have opposite signs, and the reductions do not offset exactly. BCVA therefore differs from UCVA plus UDVA.

statement: Survival-adjusted CVA and DVA formulas also capture default dependency between the two parties, so no separate correlation assumption is needed.
explanation: Survival terms are not a dependency model. The formulas assume that defaults of the two parties are independent.
originalText: The survival-adjusted formulas also capture default dependency between the two parties, so no separate correlation assumption is needed.

statement: Market practice has converged on contingent CVA and DVA: surveys show that almost all banks apply survival adjustments.
explanation: Practice is mixed rather than converged. A 2012 survey of 19 banks split between 6 using contingent and 7 using non-contingent calculations.

statement: Initial margin acts as a negative threshold: as initial margin received grows CVA tends to zero, and as the threshold grows CVA tends to its uncollateralised value.
explanation: A threshold can be seen as a negative initial margin. High thresholds leave exposure uncollateralised, while high initial margin makes collateralised CVA approach zero.
originalText: Initial margin acts as a negative threshold: as initial margin received grows, CVA tends to zero, and as the threshold grows, CVA tends to the uncollateralised value.

statement: Raising the counterparty's threshold moves CVA towards zero, because fewer margin calls means less operational exposure.
explanation: A higher threshold leaves more exposure uncollateralised, so CVA moves towards its uncollateralised value, not towards zero.
originalText: Raising the counterparty’s threshold moves CVA towards zero, because fewer margin calls means less operational exposure.

statement: Initial margin that a bank posts to its counterparty and that is held segregated reduces the bank's own CVA, because it lowers the counterparty's exposure to the bank.
explanation: Segregated initial margin the bank posts protects the counterparty and creates a margin valuation adjustment (MVA) cost for the bank. It does not reduce the bank's CVA.
originalText: Initial margin that the bank posts to the counterparty and that is held segregated reduces the bank’s CVA, because it lowers the counterparty’s exposure to the bank.

statement: A higher minimum transfer amount reduces CVA, because collateral is transferred in larger and therefore more protective amounts.
explanation: A higher MTA delays transfers and leaves more exposure uncollateralised, which increases the size of CVA.

statement: A grace (cure) period after a missed margin call is a pre-default component of the margin period of risk, while rehedging and liquidating margin securities are post-default components.
explanation: The MPoR is split into pre-default components (valuation, margin call, receiving collateral including disputes, settlement, grace period) and post-default components (macro-hedging, close-out, rehedging and liquidation of margin securities).
originalText: A grace (cure) period after a missed call is a pre-default component of the MPoR, while rehedging and liquidating margin securities are post-default.

statement: Because margin is called daily, the margin period of risk used in a CVA model should be one business day, matching the contractual period between margin calls.
explanation: Call frequency is only one component of the MPoR. Margin may be called daily while the MPoR is assumed to be, for example, 10 days.
originalText: Because margin is called daily, the model’s MPoR should be one business day, matching the contractual period between margin calls.

statement: Because the margin period of risk measures the delay in receiving margin, the same MPoR should be used to assess the funding cost of a collateralised portfolio.
explanation: The MPoR is defined assuming the counterparty defaults, so it is not relevant when assessing funding costs. Funding uses the normal, much shorter posting delay.
originalText: Because the MPoR measures the delay in receiving margin, the same MPoR should be used to assess the funding cost of the collateralised portfolio.

statement: Because the margin period of risk is the primary driver of the need for initial margin, a longer MPoR reduces the initial margin a bank should require.
explanation: A longer MPoR leaves more market risk uncollateralised, so it raises the initial margin needed.
originalText: Because the MPoR is the primary driver of the need for initial margin, a longer MPoR reduces the initial margin the bank should require.
correction: Because the margin period of risk is the primary driver of the need for initial margin, a longer MPoR increases the initial margin a bank should require.

statement: A longer margin period of risk makes collateralised CVA larger in magnitude and closer to the uncollateralised CVA, but because collateralised exposure grows with the square root of the MPoR, CVA rises by less than in proportion.
explanation: The MPoR is the window over which exposure can grow uncollateralised. Doubling it from 10 to 20 days raises exposure and CVA by about 1.41 times, not 2 times.
originalText: It becomes more negative and moves towards the uncollateralised CVA; the collateralised exposure grows with the square root of the MPoR, so the CVA rises by less than in proportion.

statement: Lengthening the margin period of risk leaves collateralised CVA unchanged as long as margin is still called daily, because the MPoR matters only for the funding of the portfolio.
explanation: Call frequency is not the MPoR, and the MPoR is a counterparty risk concept that is not used for funding. A longer MPoR increases collateralised exposure and CVA.
originalText: It is unchanged, because margin is still called daily and the MPoR matters only for the funding of the portfolio.

statement: Doubling the margin period of risk doubles the magnitude of collateralised CVA, because the uncollateralised exposure accumulates over twice as many days.
explanation: Exposure grows with the square root of time, so doubling the MPoR multiplies collateralised exposure and CVA by only about 1.41.
originalText: It doubles in magnitude, because the uncollateralised exposure accumulates over twice as many days.
